description: Three students from Phnom Penh, Cambodia, combining backend, data, frontend and finance skills to turn NASA Earth data into bilingual planting and crop-rotation guidance for Cambodian rice farmers.
summary: Field Shift KH is a bilingual (Khmer/English) interactive map that turns NASA Earth data into wet-season rice planting alerts and dry-season crop-rotation advice for all 25 Cambodian provinces. Most Cambodian rice is rain-fed, and late monsoons, dry spells and heavy rain increasingly break the traditional planting calendar, causing failed seedlings, lower yields and lost income. Using NASA POWER daily data (2000–2026) and NASA GPM IMERG satellite rainfall, the tool compares this season with the long-term normal, detects monsoon onset, flags dry-spell and heavy-rain risk, gives a 4-week soil-wetness outlook, and ranks rotation options (mungbean, maize/vegetables, green manure) by how often they would have worked in past years and by each farmer's own priorities. Traffic-light colours and plain-language advice make the results usable by farmers and extension officers. We checked POWER against IMERG, back-tested the outlook on 15,550 past cases and openly report the data's limits. Field Shift KH answers the Field Shift challenge by helping farmers adapt planting and rotation decisions to a changing climate with free NASA data.
details:
What it does

Field Shift KH is a bilingual (Khmer/English) interactive map that helps Cambodian rice farmers and agricultural extension officers decide when to plant the wet-season rice crop and what to grow in the dry season. It covers all 25 provinces. The map can be coloured by overall status, rain vs normal, monsoon onset, longest dry spell, likely soil wetness in 4 weeks, or best crop rotation. Tapping a province opens a page with a traffic-light status banner (green/yellow/red with icon and words), what to do now, the key numbers, and five sections: crop options, rain, planting time, risks and past years.

How it works

Python scripts download NASA POWER daily data (2000–2026: corrected rain, temperature and root-zone soil wetness), averaged over up to 5 grid cells per province, and NASA GPM IMERG satellite rainfall (Final Run for the normal, Late Run for this season). Rule-based logic then finds the monsoon onset (first day after 1 April with at least 20 mm of rain over 3 days and no 7-day dry spell in the next 30 days), flags dry spells and heavy rain, and builds a season-aware overall status. A 4-week outlook uses "analog years": past years that looked most like today, weighted by similarity. For the dry season, each rotation option (mungbean, maize/vegetables, green manure) is tested against every past year's weather for water (rain plus soil water, adjusted for SoilGrids soil texture) and heat limits. Options are then ranked by that reliability and by the farmer's own priorities (better soil, more income, save water, less work). The base map is built with Folium/Leaflet and published on GitHub Pages; a one-command refresh downloads new data, checks it and rebuilds the site.

Benefits and intended impact

Most Cambodian rice is rain-fed, so a late or erratic monsoon directly causes failed seedlings, lower yields and lost household income. Field Shift KH turns free NASA data, which rarely reaches farmers, into simple guidance in their own language, and helps extension officers advise whole communities. That supports fewer crop losses, better use of the dry season and stronger food security.

How we checked it

Automated data-quality checks on 245,250 rows; POWER compared with GPM IMERG (median monthly correlation 0.80); onset dates compared between the two datasets; the heavy-rain rule tested against the 2011 and 2013 Mekong floods; a sensitivity test of the onset thresholds; and a leave-one-year-out back-test of the 4-week outlook on 15,550 cases (soil-wetness skill +0.41 vs a normal year). The page shows these reliability scores per province, and 47 automated tests cover the core logic.

Tools and technologies

Python, pandas, NumPy, requests, Shapely, earthaccess and netCDF4 (NASA data download), Folium and Leaflet (map), Matplotlib, pytest, Jupyter, HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Git, GitHub and GitHub Pages. Data: NASA POWER, NASA GPM IMERG, SoilGrids, geoBoundaries and an Esri base map.

Creativity

Instead of a fixed planting calendar, the tool detects each season's actual monsoon onset from NASA data, adds a 4-week soil outlook, and goes beyond rice to rank dry-season rotations by the farmer's own priorities. All of it is delivered as Khmer-language, traffic-light guidance designed for farmers rather than scientists.

Factors we considered

Low digital literacy and language barriers (bilingual, phone-first, visual design); coarse data resolution versus small farm plots; keeping the method transparent and explainable (rule-based rather than a black-box model); being honest about data limits; and what was feasible within the hackathon.

Limitations and next steps

Thresholds are starting assumptions, not validated agronomic advice. POWER rain is modelled and has a break around 2015–2016 that makes early years too dry in the north-east and south-east. POWER and IMERG disagree in the central lowlands. The heavy-rain alert sees local rain only and is not a river-flood forecast. The Khmer text still needs checking by a native speaker. Next steps: validate the rules with farmers and agronomists, add rain-gauge data, review the Khmer text, add more crops, and send SMS alerts to basic phones.

Use of AI

Parts of the code were generated with AI assistance (Claude Code, by Anthropic) and reviewed by the team. Generated files say so in their header and in the data metadata. No NASA branding is used in AI-generated content.
